lectures.title: Blockchain in Geopolitical Competition - lesson slides
Blockchain in Geopolitical Competition - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A government loses access to major foreign payment networks and cannot easily move reserves or settle cross-border transactions. Which lesson concept best explains why this is a sovereignty problem rather than only a banking inconvenience?
questions.correct_answer: Financial rails are strategic infrastructure because they determine who can move value, settle obligations, and withstand pressure.
incorrect_answers: Cross-border networks are neutral technical pipelines because they merely route some digital transactions and automate messaging.
Domestic retail platforms are basic transactional systems because they simply support domestic payments and consumer operations.
Global messaging channels are standard utility networks because they only resolve communication issues and technical standards.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames payment and settlement access as a form of state power. Losing access can weaken reserve mobility, trade settlement, and resilience under geopolitical pressure.

questions.question_stem: A student says, "Blockchain removes governments from finance because anyone can transact on a public chain." What is the strongest correction based on the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Blockchain can reduce some legacy chokepoints while creating new control points around ledgers, exchanges, issuers, custodians, and service providers.
incorrect_answers: Blockchain can eliminate active government oversight while establishing fully autonomous networks for payments, trades, compliance, and asset management.
Blockchain can automate all regulatory enforcement while guaranteeing absolute financial privacy for users, firms, institutions, regulators, and state entities.
Blockchain can standardize global monetary policy while removing major operational dependencies on centralized issuers, banks, regulators, and local networks.
questions.explanation: The lesson's central claim is redistribution of control, not automatic decentralization. Open rails can bypass some intermediaries but often depend on visible ledgers and service-layer actors that can become chokepoints.

questions.question_stem: Which policy signal most clearly fits the lesson's description of the United States posture toward digital money?
questions.correct_answer: Favoring private digital-asset markets and regulated dollar stablecoins while resisting a federal retail CBDC.
incorrect_answers: Banning all private digital-asset platforms and decentralized payment systems while introducing a sovereign CBDC.
Promoting sovereign state-led ledgers and public payment platforms while banning private digital assets and stablecoins.
Removing legacy payment networks and banks while creating one centralized international settlement rail for every user.
questions.explanation: The United States case is described as market-led but dollar-protective: it tends to support private-sector digital assets and regulated payment stablecoins rather than a federal retail CBDC.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson pair the EU's MiCA-style rulemaking with digital euro exploration under an autonomy-oriented strategy?
questions.correct_answer: Both aim to reduce fragmentation and dependence by bringing digital finance under bloc-level supervision and resilient public-money infrastructure.
incorrect_answers: Both will seek to maximize transaction speed and scalability by deploying fully decentralized public networks and anonymous peer-to-peer applications.
Both were designed to eliminate private competition and innovation by replacing commercial bank networks with a single state-run payment utility service.
Both attempt to isolate regional financial systems from capital flows by imposing strict bans on cross-border token transactions and licensed exchanges.
questions.explanation: The EU example emphasizes supervisory integration and payment autonomy. MiCA reduces internal regulatory fragmentation, while the digital euro is tied to resilience, public money, and reduced dependence on non-European platforms.

questions.question_stem: China restricts private crypto speculation while developing state-observable digital money. What broader policy logic does the lesson assign to this combination?
questions.correct_answer: China is pursuing state-capacity control: digital money is acceptable when it remains observable and governable by state institutions.
incorrect_answers: China is actively adopting a market-led model: private stablecoins are supported when they expand cross-border trade and payment volumes.
China is promoting full decentralization: public blockchain networks are favored when they eliminate oversight by state authorities.
China is enforcing technological isolation: electronic payments are blocked when they connect domestic banking to global networks.
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses that China is not simply anti-digital-money. It is anti-uncontrolled digital money and favors state-directed, observable payment capacity through instruments such as e-CNY.

questions.question_stem: A sanctioned state experiments with digital settlement tools to keep foreign trade moving. According to the lesson, why might this strategy expand options without fully escaping pressure?
questions.correct_answer: Alternative rails may bypass some banks, but exchanges, stablecoin issuers, bridges, and enforcement coordination can recreate service-layer chokepoints.
incorrect_answers: Public ledgers may hide transaction histories, but international law enforcement and intelligence agencies can actively seize physical server hardware.
Private tokens may secure sovereign assets, but major clearing houses, commercial banks, and central authorities can dictate consensus rules directly.
Decentralized networks may eliminate domestic inflation, but regional trade organizations and market speculators can enforce absolute pricing limits.
questions.explanation: The Russia-focused discussion shows the two-sided nature of sanctions adaptation. Digital assets can provide settlement flexibility, but practical use often depends on services and counterparties exposed to monitoring or enforcement.

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson treat North Korea's crypto activity as a distinct geopolitical model rather than ordinary adoption or hub-building?
questions.correct_answer: It is framed as state-linked coercive revenue generation through theft, laundering, and sanctions-evasion activity.
incorrect_answers: It is framed as grassroots and utility-driven adoption through micro-payments, savings, and peer-to-peer transactions.
It is framed as a monitored institutional framework through compliance, licensing, and formal global integration.
It is framed as a national sovereign CBDC initiative through settlement, surveillance, and bank administration.
questions.explanation: The North Korea case is not presented as market adoption, formal regulatory integration, or CBDC development. It illustrates coercive extraction through theft and laundering.

questions.question_stem: India promotes digital rupee pilots while taxes, compliance burdens, and central-bank warnings create friction around private crypto. Which interpretation best matches the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: India is integrating digital finance cautiously by favoring state-approved innovation while discouraging but not simply banning private crypto activity.
incorrect_answers: India is pursuing absolute technological isolation by criminalizing all financial innovation while shutting down internet access for domestic retail users.
India has adopted a completely unregulated free-market model by promoting decentralized public blockchains while removing all tax and reporting rules.
India is establishing a centralized local settlement monopoly by replacing commercial banks while requiring transactions to use private stablecoins.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses India to show regulated integration with monetary caution. Official digital rails are promoted while private crypto faces friction from taxes, compliance rules, and central-bank concern.
questions.lesson_block: India: Regulated Integration With Monetary Caution

questions.question_stem: A country with high inflation and weak currency sees heavy demand for dollar-like stablecoins. Which lesson argument best explains this pattern?
questions.correct_answer: Stablecoins can become pragmatic tools for dollar access, savings, and cross-border transfer when local monetary conditions are unstable.
incorrect_answers: Stablecoins are speculative assets for rapid trading, high leverage, and short-term profit when local fiat credit markets are highly liquid.
Stablecoins can often become guaranteed tools for price stability, savings, and hedging when governments enforce strict price controls.
Stablecoins will act as direct replacements for central banks, local currencies, and payment networks when local credit markets fail.
questions.explanation: The Argentina and Nigeria examples show user-driven stablecoin demand under inflation, foreign-exchange pressure, and weak currency conditions. The lesson treats this as pragmatic adoption under economic pressure.
questions.lesson_block: Latin America And Sub-Saharan Africa: Pragmatic Adoption

questions.question_stem: A policymaker compares legacy bank rails, state digital rails, and open blockchain rails. Which conclusion most closely reflects the lesson's final comparison?
questions.correct_answer: The strategic question is which rails states trust, shape, resist, or exploit, because each rail creates different forms of dependence, visibility, scale, and control.
incorrect_answers: The primary challenge is whether open public blockchains can replace all legacy sovereign money, because digital networks naturally eliminate state regulatory power.
The central policy decision is how quickly central banks can transition to retail digital currencies, because public ledgers guarantee complete financial anonymity.
The major geopolitical concern is whether regional trade blocks can prohibit all private token exchanges, because centralized enforcement stops cross-border flows.
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by treating rail competition as unresolved. Legacy, state digital, and open blockchain rails coexist and compete over trust, scale, monetary hierarchy, and control points.

questions.question_stem: In the TRM reading, why is BLOCKINT more than simply looking at transactions on a block explorer?
questions.correct_answer: It combines on-chain data with behavioral patterns and off-chain context such as sanctions records, law-enforcement information, filings, or open-source evidence.
incorrect_answers: It replaces public ledger tracing with traditional bank wire records and centralized database access such as global SWIFT logs, domestic auditing, or client reports.
It restricts investigative focus to raw transaction volumes and token pricing histories such as market cap statistics, exchange order books, or volatility data.
This guarantees instant attribution of all address owners through cryptographic signatures and mandatory state identity registries such as passport databases.
questions.explanation: The reading distinguishes blockchain intelligence from raw tracing. BLOCKINT fuses transparent transaction data with behavioral analysis and off-chain context to support detection, attribution, and disruption.

questions.question_stem: The TRM reading describes adversaries using crypto rails while analysts also gain durable transaction records. Which statement best captures that dual-use logic?
questions.correct_answer: Crypto can help actors move value outside some bank chokepoints, but public ledgers and service-layer dependencies can create intelligence and disruption opportunities.
incorrect_answers: Crypto will allow sovereign states to completely hide illicit trade networks, but international financial agencies can instantly shut down underlying blockchain protocols.
Crypto can eliminate threat-finance risks for national security groups, but complex decentralized application systems can prevent all monitoring of cross-chain swaps.
Crypto must remain entirely outside the control of regulatory bodies, but private commercial banking databases can reveal all on-chain customer transaction details.
questions.explanation: TRM's argument aligns with the lesson's two-sided model: adversaries may use fast cross-border rails, but transparent ledgers, exchanges, issuers, brokers, and off-ramps can expose patterns and chokepoints.
questions.lesson_block: Reading: Crypto Rails As Evasion Tools And Intelligence Surfaces

questions.question_stem: After an enforcement action removes a named illicit marketplace, investigators see similar wallet patterns, liquidity sources, and interfaces appear under a new name. What reading concept does this best illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Enforcement can displace or mutate settlement networks, so behavior and infrastructure continuity may matter more than brand names alone.
incorrect_answers: Enforcement always shuts down threat-finance networks permanently, so tracking subsequent address changes is unnecessary for security teams.
Rebranding means that new virtual services are technically unrelated, so transaction records cannot provide useful investigative leads.
Regulation forces illicit participants to adopt cash settlement, so behavioral indicators can be safely ignored by security analysts.
questions.explanation: The reading emphasizes rebranding, displacement, and continuity under pressure. Sanctions or removals may create friction and signals, but functions can migrate to successor venues if demand and off-ramp channels remain.
